title: Kishkindha Kāṇḍa: The Alliance of the Vanaras
body:
Kishkindha Kāṇḍa: The Alliance of the Vanaras

He Sees Her Jewels

They came to Pampā, and it was a place of great beauty, a lake ringed with flowering trees and singing birds, lovely in the fullness of the spring, and its very loveliness was a torment to Rāma. For beauty, when the heart is grieving, does not console; it wounds. Every flowering tree reminded him of Sītā, who had loved such things; every bird’s song, every soft breeze, every sweet sight of the spring, called up her memory and sharpened his loss. Rāma walked by the beautiful lake and grieved the harder for its beauty, and spoke his sorrow aloud to Lakshmaṇa, and the tellers give us here a Rāma still raw with loss, for whom the loveliness of the world had become a kind of cruelty, each fair thing a reminder of the fairest thing he had lost.

We should not pass this by too quickly, for it is a true and tender observation about grief, and the story pauses on it deliberately. When we are happy, the beauty of the world echoes our joy; when we grieve, that same beauty can become unbearable, for it goes on being beautiful indifferent to our sorrow, and it calls up at every turn the memory of the one we have lost and the happiness we no longer have. Rāma at Pampā is every grieving soul who has ever found the spring an insult, who has walked through a beautiful day with a broken heart and hated the day for its beauty. The story lets him feel this, fully, and in letting him feel it, it honours the truth of grief and the humanity of its divine hero, who suffered the loss of his beloved exactly as we suffer ours.

But above Pampā rose the mountain Rishyamūka, and on that mountain, watching, was the one whom Kabandha had named, Sugrīva, the exiled king of the vānaras, and Sugrīva, seeing two mighty armed strangers approaching, was seized with fear.

For Sugrīva lived in exile and in terror. He had once been a prince of the vānaras, but his own brother, Vāli, the mighty king of Kishkindhā, had turned against him, had driven him out, had taken his kingdom and even his wife, and now hunted him, so that Sugrīva lived a hunted fugitive’s life on Rishyamūka, the one place Vāli could not come, ringed by a handful of faithful companions, always watching, always afraid. And now here came two strangers, armed, powerful, warriors plainly, striding toward his refuge, and Sugrīva’s fear leapt at once to the worst conclusion: that these were assassins sent by Vāli, agents of his brother, come at last to kill him even in his mountain sanctuary.

He watched them with dread, and he could not decide what to do, and it was his wisest counsellor who steadied him and resolved the matter. For among Sugrīva’s few faithful companions was one who was more than faithful, more than wise, one who was, though Sugrīva did not yet fully know it, among the greatest beings of the age: Hanumān, the son of the wind, the vānara of boundless strength and boundless devotion and boundless intelligence, who now steps for the first time into the front rank of the story and will not leave it again, for the rest of the tale is in large part his.

Do not act in fear, Hanumān counselled his master. Fear leaps to conclusions and fear is often wrong. We do not know that these strangers are enemies; they may as easily be friends. The wise course is not to flee and not to attack, but to learn the truth before deciding anything. Let me go to them, disguised, and speak with them, and discover who they are and what they want, and then we shall know whether to fear them or to welcome them. Send me first to learn the truth, and act on knowledge, not on dread.

It was wise counsel, the same wisdom that had almost been Guha’s when he faced Bharata’s army and the same that had steadied Lakshmaṇa’s suspicions, the wisdom that says: learn before you strike, discover before you decide, do not let fear write the story before the truth has spoken. And Sugrīva, trusting Hanumān as he trusted no one else, agreed, and sent Hanumān down from the mountain to meet the strangers and learn their purpose.

So Hanumān took the form of a wandering mendicant, a humble ascetic, a disguise that would let him approach the strangers without alarming them and draw them into conversation, and he went down to meet Rāma and Lakshmaṇa, all unknowing that he was going to meet the one being to whom he would devote the whole rest of his existence, the one whose service would be his glory and his joy and his very meaning, the Lord for whom, from this meeting onward, Hanumān would do the impossible again and again, leaping oceans and lifting mountains and carrying in his single faithful heart the hope of the whole cause. The wind’s son went down the mountain to spy out two strangers, and he came back having found his god, though neither he nor Rāma yet knew what this meeting was, or all that it would come to mean.

And there is a fitness in it, the tellers say, that Hanumān came first as a humble mendicant, in disguise, in service to another’s need, cautious and courteous and wise. For that is what Hanumān was, beneath his boundless power: a servant, the perfect servant, whose whole greatness lay in devotion, in the pouring-out of his enormous gifts not for himself but for those he loved and served. He came in the guise of humility because humility was his truth, and he came in service because service was his nature, and the greatest of the vānaras stepped into the story bowing, in disguise, seeking not to display his power but to learn how he might help. It is the perfect introduction to the perfect devotee, and everything that Hanumān would become, the leaper of oceans, the burner of Lankā, the bearer of mountains, was already present in that first humble, careful, self-effacing approach, the servant going quietly down the mountain to learn how he might serve.

The meeting was about to take place that would bind Rāma and Sugrīva and Hanumān together, would turn the tide of the whole story, would set in motion the great search and the great war, and would begin the friendship, between Rāma and Hanumān, that is perhaps the most beautiful thing in all this beautiful and terrible tale. Down the mountain the wind’s son went, in his mendicant’s disguise, toward the two grieving strangers by the beautiful cruel lake, and the next age of the story began.

Sugrīva’s Doubts Cleared

Hanumān came to the two strangers in his mendicant’s disguise, and he spoke to them, and from the first words a kind of recognition passed between them, for Hanumān was wise, and Rāma was Rāma, and each perceived at once that here was no ordinary being. Hanumān’s speech was so eloquent, so graceful, so perfectly courteous and well-ordered, that Rāma marvelled at it, and remarked to Lakshmaṇa that one who could speak so must be a being of the highest cultivation, that such command of language betokened a mind of rare quality. And Hanumān, for his part, drawing the strangers out, learned their story: that this was Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā, whose wife had been carried off by a demon, who sought allies for her recovery, and who had been directed to Sugrīva by the dying Kabandha.

And when Hanumān understood who these were and what they sought, his disguise and his caution fell away, for he saw at once that here was no threat to Sugrīva but the very salvation of him, an ally sent as if by destiny, one whose need matched Sugrīva’s own and whose power could restore everything Sugrīva had lost. He revealed himself, and told them of Sugrīva, of his exile and his wrongs, of how his brother Vāli had driven him out and taken his kingdom and his wife, and of how Sugrīva too longed for an ally who could help him regain what he had lost. Here, Hanumān saw, was a friendship made in heaven: two wronged and exiled princes, each having lost a wife and a home, each needing exactly what the other could provide. And Hanumān, overjoyed, took the brothers up the mountain to meet Sugrīva, and so the alliance began.

Sugrīva and Rāma met, and their meeting was warm, for each recognized in the other a fellow-sufferer and a natural ally, and they resolved to make a pact of friendship, and they made it in the most solemn way, before fire. They kindled a sacred flame, and around it they swore friendship and alliance, each pledging to help the other recover what he had lost: Rāma would help Sugrīva defeat Vāli and regain his kingdom and his wife; Sugrīva would place his vast host of vānaras at Rāma’s service to search for Sītā and to help recover her. It was a pact sealed by fire, the most binding of oaths, and it bound the two of them and their causes together from that moment on.

And Sugrīva, his hope kindled, showed Rāma something he had kept: for he had been among those on the mountaintop when Rāvaṇa flew over carrying Sītā, and he had seen the bundle of jewels she had dropped, and had gathered it up and kept it. Now he brought it out and showed it to Rāma, the ornaments Sītā had cast down as a sign. And Rāma, seeing them, knew them for Sītā’s, and was overcome again with grief and love, holding the jewels of his lost wife, the first tangible trace of her he had found, the proof that she had passed this way, that she lived, that she had been carried south exactly as Jaṭāyu had said. He pressed the jewels to him and wept over them, and the sight of his grief moved Sugrīva and Hanumān and bound them the more firmly to his cause.

But there was a difficulty, and Sugrīva, though he had made the pact, was troubled by a doubt, and his doubt was reasonable, and the clearing of it is the heart of this chapter. For Sugrīva had pledged to help Rāma, but Rāma had pledged to help Sugrīva against Vāli, and Vāli was terrible. Vāli was the mightiest of all the vānaras, of a strength that was legendary, and Sugrīva had fled from him in helpless terror and lived as a hunted exile precisely because he could not stand against his brother’s power. And now here was Rāma, promising to defeat this same Vāli; but Rāma was a stranger, a man, and Sugrīva did not yet know whether even Rāma’s strength was equal to Vāli’s. He had staked everything on this alliance, but a whisper of doubt remained: was this ally, for all his noble bearing, actually strong enough to do what he promised? Or would Sugrīva, trusting him, find himself once more facing his terrible brother with a champion who could not match him?

Rāma understood the doubt, and did not resent it, for it was fair, and he resolved to answer it not with words but with proof. And so he performed two feats that swept away every trace of Sugrīva’s hesitation, and they are famous.

Sugrīva showed Rāma the enormous skeleton of a demon named Dundubhi, a monstrous buffalo-demon whom Vāli had slain long ago and whose vast dry bones still lay where they had fallen. It was a measure of Vāli’s strength that he had killed so mighty a creature; and Sugrīva, showing the huge skeleton, meant to convey what Rāma was up against. And Rāma, for answer, simply walked to the enormous skeleton, and with a single kick of his foot, sent the whole vast mass of bones flying through the air, hurling it an immense distance, tossing that monstrous skeleton as a child might toss a ball. It was a display of casual, overwhelming strength, and Sugrīva’s eyes widened at it, but a shadow of doubt remained, for he noted, shrewdly, that Vāli had killed Dundubhi when the demon was alive and in his full power, whereas Rāma had only flung the dry dead bones; the feats were not quite equal.

So Rāma gave him a second proof, and this one left no room for any doubt at all. Nearby stood a row of seven great sāl trees, mighty trunks in a line. And Rāma took up his bow, and fitted a single arrow, and drew, and loosed, and the one arrow passed clean through all seven of the enormous trees, one after another, piercing every one, and passed on through the earth beyond, and, the tellers say, returned to Rāma’s quiver. Seven great trees pierced by a single shaft: it was a feat beyond anything Vāli could do, beyond anything Sugrīva had ever seen or imagined, a display of power so far past the ordinary that it could only belong to a being more than mortal.

And with that, Sugrīva’s every doubt was swept away, and his hesitation turned to a joyful, overwhelming faith. He understood now that his ally was no ordinary warrior, however noble, but a power against which even the terrible Vāli was as nothing, and that in binding himself to Rāma he had bound himself to certain victory. He fell at Rāma’s feet, filled with awe and gratitude and hope, ready now to go against his brother without fear, certain that with such a champion beside him his long exile was ending and his stolen kingdom and wife would be restored. The pact was sealed, the doubt was cleared, the alliance was firm, and the two wronged princes, each strengthened by the other, turned now toward the first task their friendship required: the challenging of Vāli, and the terrible, morally troubling combat that would end in the death of the mightiest of the vānaras and the restoration of Sugrīva to his throne.

The Slaying of Vāli

The plan was simple in its outline. Sugrīva would go to Kishkindhā and challenge Vāli to single combat, and while the brothers fought, Rāma, hidden nearby, would loose the arrow that would slay Vāli, and so Sugrīva would be freed of his terrible brother and restored to his kingdom. But the carrying-out of it went wrong the first time, and the going-wrong, and the setting-right, and above all the deep moral question that the whole episode raises, make this one of the most debated chapters in the entire epic.

Sugrīva went and challenged Vāli, and Vāli came out, and the two brothers fought, and they fought with such fury and such likeness that Rāma, watching from his hiding place, bow drawn, could not tell them apart. For the two vānara brothers were so alike in form, grappling and wheeling in the dust of their combat, that Rāma dared not loose his arrow for fear of striking Sugrīva instead of Vāli. And so he held his hand, and the fight went on, and Vāli, far the stronger, beat Sugrīva badly, and Sugrīva, wounded and bewildered that his ally had not struck, broke off and fled back to Rāma in dismay.

Why did you not shoot, Sugrīva demanded, wounded and reproachful. You promised, and I trusted you, and I went against my brother on the strength of that promise, and he nearly killed me, and your arrow never came. And Rāma explained: I could not tell you apart. You are so alike that I feared to strike you instead of him. Go again, but this time wear something to distinguish yourself, some token, some garland, so that I may know you in the fight and strike the right brother. And so it was arranged; Hanumān, or another, placed a garland of flowers about Sugrīva’s neck, so that in the second combat Rāma could tell the brothers apart.

Sugrīva went again, and challenged Vāli again, and again the brothers fought, and this time Rāma, watching, could see the garland and know his friend, and when the moment came he drew his bow and loosed his arrow from his hiding place, and the shaft flew true and struck Vāli in the chest, and the mightiest of the vānaras fell.

And now comes the moment that has troubled thoughtful readers for as long as this story has been told, for Vāli, lying mortally wounded, did not die quietly, but turned upon Rāma with a bitter and a powerful accusation, and the accusation was not easy to answer. Rāma came out from his hiding place, and Vāli, dying, looked up at him and challenged his righteousness to his face. You are Rāma, Vāli said, or such was the sense of his dying words, prince of the great house of Ikshvāku, renowned through all the world for your justice, your virtue, your unfailing dharma. Men speak your name as the very measure of righteousness. And how have you used that righteousness against me? You have shot me from hiding, from ambush, while I was engaged in combat with another and had no quarrel with you and did not even see you. I had done you no wrong. I had never harmed you or yours. You had no cause against me. And yet you, the mirror of dharma, struck me down from concealment, like a hunter shooting a beast at a watering-place, without warning, without challenge, without giving me any chance to face you. Where is your vaunted righteousness in this? What law of the warrior, what code of honour, permits a king to shoot from ambush a creature that has done him no wrong? You have stained your great name with a coward’s deed, and I, dying, demand to know how you justify it.

It was a formidable accusation, and its force is real, and the story does not pretend it is not. Rāma had killed from hiding a being who had no quarrel with him; on its face, it looks exactly like the injustice Vāli names. And Rāma’s answer, the justification he gives, is one of the most searching passages of moral reasoning in the whole epic, and it repays close attention, for it is Rāma reasoning his way through a genuine hard case, as he always does, refusing to let the matter rest on mere power or mere assertion.

Rāma knelt beside the dying Vāli and answered him. Hear me, he said, for you deserve an answer, and I will give you a true one. You accuse me of injustice, but consider what you have done, and what my duty is. You have committed a grave sin, a sin against the very order of dharma, for you drove out your own brother and, while he yet lived, you took his wife to yourself. To take a brother’s wife while the brother lives is among the gravest of transgressions; by the law it is a monstrous thing, a violation of the moral order at its root, and by that act you reduced yourself, king though you were, to the level of a beast that knows no such law. Now I am of the house of Ikshvāku, and it is the ancient duty of our line to uphold dharma across the earth, to punish transgression wherever it is found, even in kingdoms not our own, for the kings of my line are the appointed guardians of the moral order. You had committed a sin that merited punishment, and it fell to me, as the upholder of dharma, to punish it. That is the first answer: I struck you not without cause but as the just punishment of a real and grievous wrong.

And as for the manner of it, the shooting from hiding, Rāma went on, consider this too. You are not a man, bound by the codes of combat between warriors; you are a vānara, one of the forest creatures, and men hunt the creatures of the forest, and it is no violation of dharma to take such a creature by whatever means, from hiding or in the open, as hunters have always done. But more than that: your strength is such that no one could stand against you in open combat; that is the whole reason your brother fled you and could not face you. Had I challenged you openly, you would simply have overpowered me or fled, and the punishment your sin required would never have been accomplished. To punish a transgressor too mighty to be taken in open fight, the just may use the means that will serve, as the hunter uses concealment against the strong beast. The end was just, and the means were such as the case allowed.

Now we must be honest, as the story is honest, that not every reader has found Rāma’s answer wholly satisfying, and the debate over the killing of Vāli has never entirely been settled, and perhaps is not meant to be. There is a discomfort in it that the reasoning does not entirely dissolve, and the story seems to want us to feel that discomfort, to wrestle with it, rather than to accept a pat resolution. For here is one of the deep purposes of the episode: it shows us that even Rāma, even the very measure of righteousness, operates in a world where dharma is not always simple, where the right course is not always clean, where the upholding of the moral order may require acts that trouble the conscience even as they serve justice. The world is not tidy. Even the best of men, doing his genuine best to serve the right, may act in ways that a good conscience can question. And the story, by giving Vāli so strong an accusation and Rāma so reasoned but not wholly comfortable an answer, refuses to pretend that righteousness is ever easy or that the servant of dharma escapes the hard ambiguities of action in a fallen world. This is not a flaw in the story; it is its honesty, its refusal to make Rāma a figure of easy perfection rather than a soul genuinely wrestling, as we all must, with the terrible difficulty of doing right.

And Vāli himself, in the end, was satisfied, and this matters, for the one who had most cause to condemn Rāma came, in his dying, to accept the justice of what had been done. Hearing Rāma’s answer, understanding at last the gravity of his own sin and the justice of his punishment, the deeper truth of the moral order he had violated, Vāli’s bitterness left him. He acknowledged the rightness of Rāma’s words, begged forgiveness for his own transgression and for his hard accusation, and, dying, entrusted to Rāma’s care the thing he loved most in the world, his son Angada, asking that the boy be protected and cherished. And so Vāli died reconciled, his enmity dissolved into understanding, commending his son to the very one whose arrow had slain him, at peace at the last with the justice that had brought him down. And Rāma received the charge of Angada, and honoured it, and the mightiest of the vānaras passed from the world, leaving his kingdom to the brother he had wronged and his son to the guardianship of the Lord who had judged him.

Tārā’s Grief

Vāli was dead, and Kishkindhā, which had exulted under his mighty rule, was plunged into mourning, and at the centre of the mourning stood his widow, Tārā, and her grief is one of the great laments of the epic, and her character one of its most admirable.

Tārā was Vāli’s queen, and she was no ordinary consort. She was wise, wise beyond most of the counsellors of the kingdom, and it is said that she had warned Vāli against the very combat that killed him, had counselled him not to go out against Sugrīva a second time, for she had reasoned shrewdly that Sugrīva would not have dared to challenge his mighty brother again unless he had gained some powerful ally, and that the wise course was caution, not the headlong pride that sent Vāli out to his death. He had not listened. The mighty seldom listen to the counsel of caution, and Vāli in his strength had scorned his wise wife’s warning and gone out and died, and now Tārā’s wisdom was vindicated in the bitterest way, by the death she had foreseen and failed to prevent.

She came to where Vāli lay dying, or dead, and she cast herself upon his body, and she wept, and her lament is long and moving in the telling, the grief of a wise woman for a husband she had loved and warned and lost. She did not rail against fate as a foolish woman might; her grief was deep but it was not without understanding; she saw the whole shape of the tragedy, her husband’s pride, her own unheeded warning, the working-out of a doom that wisdom had glimpsed and love had been unable to avert. And she ignored, in her grief, the whole business of the kingdom that swirled around her, the questions of succession and power that Vāli’s death had thrown open; she cared nothing, in that hour, for who would rule; she cared only that her husband was dead, and she mourned him with her whole heart, with a dignity that commanded the respect even of those who had brought about his fall.

There is a particular poignancy in Tārā’s grief, and it is worth dwelling on, for it is the grief of the wise who could not save what they loved. There is a special anguish in having seen the danger clearly, in having spoken the warning, in having done all that wisdom could do, and in watching the loved one walk past the warning into the very doom you foresaw. Tārā had that anguish. She had known; she had said; and it had not been enough; and now she must grieve not only for her husband but for the terrible uselessness of her own clear sight, for the warning that was true and was not heeded. It is among the hardest of human sorrows, to be right and to be helpless, to see the cliff and be unable to turn the beloved from it, and Tārā bore that sorrow, and the story honours her for the dignity with which she bore it.

And there was young Angada, Vāli’s son, the boy whom the dying Vāli had entrusted to Rāma’s care, and his grief too was terrible, the grief of a son suddenly fatherless, and the fear of a prince suddenly uncertain of his place in a kingdom passing to his uncle. The whole royal house of the vānaras was thrown into confusion and sorrow by the fall of its mighty king, and for a while it seemed that grief and uncertainty might tear the kingdom apart.

But order had to be restored, for a kingdom cannot mourn forever, and the living must arrange the affairs the dead leave behind. And here Rāma’s justice showed itself again, and his care for the proper order of things. Vāli was dead, and by right the kingdom now passed to Sugrīva, whom Vāli had wronged, and Sugrīva was crowned king of Kishkindhā at last, restored to the throne from which his brother had driven him, his long exile ended. But Rāma was careful that the restoration should be just and complete, and that the innocent should not suffer for the quarrels of the mighty. And so it was arranged, at Rāma’s wise insistence, that young Angada, Vāli’s son, should not be cast aside or disinherited, but should be made the crown prince, the Yuvarāja, the heir apparent to Sugrīva’s throne. So the boy who had lost his father did not also lose his future; the succession was secured for him; and the kingdom was reunited, Sugrīva as king and Angada as heir, the two branches of the royal house joined again rather than set at war.

This was a wise and a merciful settlement, and it is worth marking what it accomplished. Vāli’s death might have left a legacy of bitterness, a wronged widow, a disinherited son, a kingdom divided between the partisans of the dead king and the partisans of the new. Instead, by honouring Vāli’s son, by securing Angada’s place, by treating the defeated house with justice and generosity rather than with the harshness that victory so often shows, Rāma and Sugrīva healed the division rather than deepening it, and bound the whole kingdom together in the new order rather than leaving it split. It is the mark of true statecraft, and true righteousness, to be generous in victory, to secure the place of the defeated rather than to crush them, to heal rather than to punish; and this healing settlement, with the wronged widow honoured and the fatherless son made heir, is the fruit of Rāma’s insistence that even in the aftermath of a necessary death, justice and mercy should govern the arrangements of the living.

And Tārā herself, the wise widow, was honoured and given her due place, her wisdom respected, her dignity preserved. She would appear again in the story, her counsel still valued, her clear sight still serving the kingdom that had lost her husband; for a woman of such wisdom was too valuable to be set aside, and the new order had the sense to keep her honoured and near. Her grief did not destroy her; she carried it, as the wise carry their sorrows, and went on, diminished but not broken, to lend her wisdom to the cause that her husband’s death had joined her to.

So the storm of Vāli’s death passed, and out of it came a new settlement: Sugrīva king, Angada his heir, Tārā honoured, the kingdom reunited and at peace, and, most important for our story, the whole vast power of the vānaras now pledged to Rāma’s cause. For this had been the purpose of the whole hard business, the reason Rāma had bound himself to Sugrīva and undertaken the troubling slaying of Vāli: to gain an ally who could command the hosts of the vānaras and send them across the earth in search of Sītā. Now that ally was king, secure on his throne, in Rāma’s debt, bound by the pact of fire, and the way was open at last for the great search to begin.

Or so it should have been. But Sugrīva, restored to his throne and his kingdom and his pleasures after his long hard exile, was about to forget, in the sweetness of his recovered fortune, the debt he owed and the promise he had sworn, and the great search that should have begun at once would be delayed, and the delay would rouse a wrath that shook the palace of Kishkindhā to its foundations.

Anger and Reconciliation

The rains came. In that country the monsoon fell in a great unbroken deluge that made all movement impossible, that turned the rivers to torrents and the paths to mud and shut the world indoors for months, and it was agreed, reasonably enough, that the search for Sītā could not begin until the rains had passed, for no host could march through such weather. So Rāma and Lakshmaṇa withdrew to a cave on a hillside near Kishkindhā to wait out the monsoon, and Sugrīva returned to his palace and his kingdom, and the two waited, in their very different circumstances, for the rains to end and the search to begin.

And the difference between those two circumstances is the heart of this chapter, and it is drawn with a deliberate and painful contrast. In the cave on the hill, Rāma waited in sorrow. The rains, the enforced idleness, the long wet months with nothing to do but wait, were a torment to him, for every day that passed was a day of Sītā’s captivity, a day of her suffering in the hands of the demon, and Rāma could do nothing but wait and grieve and long for the weather to break so that the search could begin. The monsoon that shut the world indoors shut him in with his grief, and he passed those months in an agony of impatience and sorrow, counting the days, aching for his lost wife, the beauty of the rain-washed world only sharpening his loss as the beauty of Pampā had sharpened it.

And in the palace of Kishkindhā, Sugrīva forgot.

For Sugrīva, restored to everything he had lost, drowned in the sweetness of his recovered fortune. He had his kingdom back, and his throne, and his wife, and all the pleasures of a great king, after long years of hunted exile, and the sudden reversal from misery to luxury overwhelmed him. He gave himself up to enjoyment, to feasting, to wine, to the delights of his recovered palace and his recovered queens, and in the intoxication of his pleasures he forgot, simply forgot, the debt he owed and the promise he had sworn. The rains gave him an excuse to do nothing, and pleasure gave him a reason to want to do nothing, and between the two he let the whole matter of Sītā and the search slip out of his mind, and passed the monsoon in indulgence while Rāma grieved in the cave, and even when the rains ended he did not stir, so lost was he in his recovered pleasures.

Let us pause on this, for it is a sharp and unsparing portrait of a real human failing, and the story means it as a warning. Sugrīva was not a wicked man. He had suffered genuinely; his joy at his restoration was natural; who could blame a man, long miserable, for delighting in his recovered fortune? And yet in that delight he committed a real wrong, the wrong of forgetting, the wrong of the man who, once his own troubles are eased, forgets the friend to whom he owes his easing and the promise by which his own good fortune was bought. Rāma had given Sugrīva everything, his kingdom, his throne, his wife, his life; and Sugrīva, once he had them, forgot the giver and the price. It is a common failing, and a grievous one, this forgetting of our debts in the comfort of our satisfaction, this letting-slip of our obligations once our own needs are met, and the story holds it up in Sugrīva as a thing to be ashamed of, a lapse that nearly cost him everything and that certainly cost him his honour for a season. Prosperity, the story warns, can corrupt as surely as adversity, can make us forgetful and indulgent and false to our word, and the man who keeps faith in his misery may break it in his comfort, and that is a shameful thing.

And the ending of the rains, which should have been the signal for the search to begin, passed unmarked in Kishkindhā, and still Sugrīva did not stir, and word of his continued indulgence reached the cave, and Lakshmaṇa’s wrath, which we have seen before, kindled now to a terrible blaze.

For Lakshmaṇa could not bear it, this betrayal, this ingratitude, this drunken forgetting while his brother grieved. That Sugrīva, who owed everything to Rāma, should wallow in his pleasures and forget his sworn duty while Sītā suffered and Rāma broke his heart in a cave, filled Lakshmaṇa with a fury that would not be contained. He took up his bow, and he marched to Kishkindhā, to the very palace, in a rage that shook the ground, his bowstring twanging, his whole being blazing with the anger of a loyal heart betrayed, meaning to call Sugrīva to account, and, if the false king would not answer, to deal with him as an oath-breaker deserved. The palace of Kishkindhā trembled at his coming, for the wrath of Lakshmaṇa was a fearful thing, and the vānaras fled before him, and it seemed that the alliance itself might be about to end in blood and the ingrate Sugrīva to pay for his forgetting with his life.

And here, in the crisis, it was again a wise woman who stepped forward to prevent catastrophe, and it was Tārā, Vāli’s widow, the wise queen who had passed now into Sugrīva’s keeping and counsel. For Tārā, seeing Lakshmaṇa’s terrible wrath and understanding the danger, went out to meet him, calmly, with dignity, and she faced the raging prince where the frightened vānaras had fled, and she spoke to him with such grace and such reason that she disarmed his fury.

Do not yield to anger, noble prince, she said, or such was the sense of her words. Your anger is just; Sugrīva has done wrong; I do not deny it. He has been at fault; he has forgotten himself in his pleasures; the delay is a real fault and a shameful one. But consider: his love for Rāma is true, beneath his forgetting; his fault is weakness, not treachery; he has been overwhelmed by his sudden fortune, not turned false in his heart. And consider too that a great enterprise like the search you plan is not so easily begun, that the gathering of the vast hosts of the vānaras from all the corners of the earth takes time and preparation, and that even now the work may be further along than your anger supposes. Do not destroy the alliance in a moment of just wrath; do not let a real but forgivable fault become the ruin of the whole cause. Give Sugrīva the chance to make amends, and you will find him eager to fulfill his promise; strike him down in anger, and you lose the very ally whose help you need. Let justice be tempered with patience; let the fault be corrected rather than punished; and the search will go forward, and Sītā will be sought, and all will be well.

Her eloquence, her calm, her wisdom, and above all the manifest truth of what she said, reached through Lakshmaṇa’s fury and quieted it, as her counsel and her grace had a power that raw force could not have had. Lakshmaṇa’s wrath cooled; he saw the justice of her words; he saw that to destroy the alliance would serve no one and doom Sītā; and he consented to give Sugrīva the chance to make amends. And Sugrīva, roused at last from his indulgence, shaken to his senses by the near-disaster his forgetting had brought upon him, was overcome with remorse. He came to Lakshmaṇa, and to Rāma, full of shame and apology, acknowledging his fault, begging forgiveness, and, most important, moving at once to make good his broken promise. He would begin the search this very hour; he would summon the vānara hosts from every quarter of the earth; he would pour the whole strength of his kingdom into the finding of Sītā, and make amends for his shameful delay by the vigour of his repentance.

And so the crisis passed, the anger was reconciled, the alliance held, and the great search, so long delayed by rain and by forgetting, was at last set in motion. Sugrīva, restored to his duty by the near-loss of everything, summoned the vānaras, and they came, a host beyond counting, gathering from all the corners of the world at their king’s command, until the whole country around Kishkindhā swarmed with the mustering armies of the monkey-people, ready at last to be sent forth in the four directions to search the whole earth for the hidden Sītā. The forgetting was forgiven, the debt was being paid, and the search for the lost queen was about to begin in earnest.

The Search Begins

The vānara hosts assembled, a multitude beyond counting, gathered from every mountain and forest of the world, and Sugrīva divided them into four great search parties and sent them forth in the four directions, north and south, east and west, to search the whole earth for Sītā. To each party he gave a time, a term within which they must return, and detailed instructions of the lands they were to search, for Sugrīva, who had wandered the whole world as a hunted exile, knew its far countries better than any, and he described to each party the regions it was to explore, the mountains and rivers and hidden places, with a knowledge that astonished those who heard it.

But it was upon the southern party that the whole hope of the search rested, though none of them yet knew it, for it was to the south that Rāvaṇa had carried Sītā, and it was the southern party that would find her trail. And Sugrīva, whether by wisdom or by some prompting of destiny, put into that southern party his very best: Angada, the young crown prince, Vāli’s son, as its nominal leader; the wise old bear Jāmbavān, ancient and full of counsel; and, above all, Hanumān, the son of the wind, in whom, though few yet knew it, lay the power to accomplish what no other could. Rāma, sensing something, or trusting Hanumān above all the others, gave to Hanumān a token, his signet ring, to carry, so that if Hanumān should find Sītā, he might show her the ring and she would know him for a true messenger of Rāma. It was to Hanumān that Rāma entrusted his ring, and there is a fitness in it, for it was Hanumān who would need it.

The southern party set out, and searched, and their search was long and hard and for a great while fruitless. They ranged across the southern lands, through forests and over mountains, searching everywhere, finding nothing, and the term Sugrīva had given them began to run short, and despair began to creep upon them, for to return without having found Sītā, and moreover to return after the appointed time, was to face Sugrīva’s anger and to have failed the whole great cause.

And in the midst of their searching, they met with an adventure that the tellers preserve and that Vishṇu Sreenivas had passed over in his condensed telling, but that belongs to the fullness of the tale, and is restored here: the adventure of the enchanted cave and the ascetic woman Swayamprabhā.

For the southern party, wandering in their search, came upon a great cave in the mountains, and being weary and thirsty, and seeing signs that water might lie within, they entered it. And the cave was no ordinary cave; it was vast, and it was dark, and it wound on and on into the mountain, deeper and deeper, until the searchers were lost in its endless windings, groping in a darkness that seemed to have no end, and they feared that they had trapped themselves, that they would wander in that lightless labyrinth until they died, and that their search and their lives would end together in the belly of the mountain.

But as they groped on in despair, they saw at last a light ahead, and following it they came into a wondrous place, a whole hidden world within the mountain, a magical realm of light and beauty, with gardens and pools and golden palaces, lit as if by its own sun, a paradise concealed in the heart of the rock. It was a marvel beyond anything they had seen, and they wandered through it in astonishment, and at its heart they found its keeper: an ascetic woman, aged, radiant, of great spiritual power, seated in devotion. Her name was Swayamprabhā, and she guarded this hidden realm, which had been made long ago by a celestial architect and left in her keeping.

The vānaras were afraid, and hungry, and lost, and she received them with kindness. She fed them, for the enchanted realm held fruit and water in abundance, and she let them rest and recover their strength, and she asked them their story, and they told her: of Rāma, and of stolen Sītā, and of their search, and of how they had blundered into the cave and lost themselves in its darkness and feared they would never find their way out to complete their task. And Swayamprabhā, moved by their story and their plight, resolved to help them, and she did a thing that only her great spiritual power could do. Close your eyes, she told them; and when they had closed their eyes, by her yogic power, in an instant, she transported the whole party out of the enchanted cave and set them down upon the shore of the southern sea, far away, at the very edge of the ocean, exactly where they needed to be to continue their search. They opened their eyes and found themselves out of the mountain, out of the darkness, delivered by her grace to the seashore, their strength restored, their way clear, saved from the labyrinth that would have been their tomb.

There is a grace in this small restored episode, and it is worth marking, for it belongs to the pattern of the whole story: that the searchers, lost and despairing in the darkness, were saved not by their own strength but by an unlooked-for kindness, by the grace of a holy being who fed them and delivered them and set them on their way. Again and again in this tale, help comes from unexpected quarters, from a hunter-chief, a dying bird, an old tribal woman, and now an ascetic hermit-woman in a hidden cave; and again and again it is the humble and the holy, off the great road of the mighty, who give the crucial aid. Swayamprabhā asked nothing, gained nothing, and gave everything the searchers needed, and vanished from the story as quietly as she had entered it, one more of the many quiet helpers whose small graces, added together, make the great victory possible. The search for Sītā was not the work of Rāma alone, nor of the vānara armies alone, but of a whole chain of kindnesses, humble and often unremembered, and Swayamprabhā’s deliverance of the lost searchers is one link in that long chain of grace.

But the searchers, delivered to the seashore, now faced a new despair, and a worse one. For they had been set down at the edge of the ocean, and beyond the ocean, they now understood, must lie Lankā and Sītā, but the ocean was vast, a hundred leagues of open sea, and no vānara among them could cross it. And worse, the term Sugrīva had given them had now expired; they had spent too long in their wandering and their adventure in the cave; they had passed the appointed time; and they had not found Sītā, only reached the shore of the sea that barred them from her. To return now was to return late and empty- handed, to face Sugrīva’s wrath and to have failed; to go on was impossible, for the sea could not be crossed. Trapped between an impossible ocean and an angry king, their term expired and their goal beyond their reach, the southern party sank into the deepest despair of the whole search, and some of them resolved that they would not return at all, that they would rather fast to death there on the shore than go back as failures, and they prepared themselves to die by the edge of the sea that had defeated them.

And it was in that extremity, at the very bottom of their despair, on the shore of the impassable ocean, that the two things happened that would turn the whole story: the coming of a great bird with knowledge of Sītā, and the rousing, at last, of the sleeping power of Hanumān.

Son of Vāyu

As the despairing searchers sat by the shore preparing to die, their loud lamentations, and in particular the name of Jaṭāyu spoken among them, drew the attention of a great old bird who dwelt nearby, and he came to them, and he was Sampāti, and he was the elder brother of Jaṭāyu, and his coming was the first of the two wonders that saved the search.

Sampāti was an ancient vulture, huge and aged, and he had lost his wings long ago, in his youth, when he and his brother Jaṭāyu had flown too near the sun and Sampāti, shielding his younger brother from the burning heat with his own body, had had his wings scorched away, and had fallen to earth, and had lived ever since, wingless, upon that shore. He heard the vānaras speaking of Jaṭāyu, and he came to them eager for news of his brother, and they told him, sorrowfully, of Jaṭāyu’s death, of how the old bird had fought Rāvaṇa to save Sītā and been slain for it. And Sampāti grieved for his brother, but he was proud, too, that Jaṭāyu had died so nobly, in so good a cause, and out of gratitude for the news and admiration for his brother’s sacrifice, he resolved to help the searchers with the one thing he could give them, which was knowledge.

For Sampāti, though wingless, had the far sight of the great birds, a vision that could see across enormous distances, and he had, moreover, seen the very thing they sought. I have seen her, he told them. With my far sight I have seen, across the sea, in the golden city of Lankā, in a grove of ashoka trees, a woman held captive, grieving, guarded by demons, and by all you have told me she can be no other than your Sītā. She is there, across this ocean, in Lankā, the city of Rāvaṇa, held in the Ashokavana. I have seen her with my own far- seeing eyes. There is your goal; there is the captive you seek; she lives, and she is there, across the water.

This was the breakthrough, the thing the whole long search had been for: certain knowledge of where Sītā was. Sampāti’s far sight had accomplished what all the searching of the vānara hosts had not; he had located Sītā precisely, named her prison, confirmed that she lived. The despair of the shore lifted; the search had succeeded; they knew now where she was. And there is a fitness, the tellers note, in the two brothers, Jaṭāyu and Sampāti, bracketing the search: Jaṭāyu at the beginning, whose dying words told Rāma who had taken Sītā and in what direction; Sampāti at the end, whose far sight told the searchers exactly where she had been carried. The two old birds, brothers, each gave the crucial knowledge at the crucial moment, and between them they framed the whole finding of Sītā, so that the search that began with one brother’s dying testimony was completed by the other brother’s living sight.

But knowing where Sītā was and reaching her were two different things, for the ocean still lay between, a hundred leagues of open sea, and no vānara could cross it. They knew now that Sītā was in Lankā; but Lankā was across that impassable water; and knowledge without the power to act on it is only a sharper kind of helplessness. The searchers looked at the vast sea and despaired anew, for which of them could leap a hundred leagues of ocean? They tried to reckon it among themselves, each naming how far he could leap, and the answers fell pitifully short; the greatest leapers among them could manage but a fraction of the distance; not one could cross that sea; and it seemed that they had found Sītā only to be stopped forever at the water’s edge, able to see her prison in their minds and utterly unable to reach it.

And here occurred the second wonder, the rousing of Hanumān, and it is one of the most beloved moments in the whole epic, for it is the moment when the greatest of the vānaras discovered, or rather was reminded of, what he truly was.

For Hanumān had sat silent through all this reckoning of leaps, not naming his own power, and this was because Hanumān did not know his own power, or had forgotten it. There is a story behind this forgetting: that Hanumān, as a child, had been so mighty and so mischievous, his strength so boundless and so dangerous in one who did not know how to govern it, that the sages had laid upon him a kind of forgetting, a veil upon his own knowledge of his powers, so that he would not know his full strength until the moment came when he needed it and was reminded of it. And so Hanumān had gone through his life not knowing what he truly was, this greatest of beings walking humbly among the others, his boundless power sleeping within him, hidden even from himself.

And now the wise old bear Jāmbavān, who was ancient and knew many things, saw that the moment had come, and he went to Hanumān, and he roused him. Why do you sit silent, Hanumān, he said, as though this task were beyond you? Do you not know what you are? Do you not know your own birth and your own power? You are the son of Vāyu, the wind-god himself; the wind is your father; and there is no distance you cannot cross, no leap beyond your power, for the strength of the wind is in you, boundless, and you have only forgotten it. Remember yourself, son of the wind. Remember what you are. This sea is nothing to you; this hundred leagues is a stride for you; you alone of all of us can make this crossing, for you alone are the child of the wind and heir to his boundless power. Rise, and remember, and grow, and leap, and carry the hope of us all across the sea to Lankā and to Sītā.

And as Jāmbavān spoke, the veil lifted, and Hanumān remembered. The knowledge of his own nature came back to him, the memory of his divine birth and his boundless power, and with the knowledge came the power itself, waking in him, swelling, rising. And Hanumān began to grow. Before the astonished eyes of the whole search party, the humble vānara who had sat silent among them began to expand, to swell, to increase, growing vaster and vaster, his form enlarging until he was a giant, a colossus, a mountain of a being, his strength blazing up in him as he remembered at last the full truth of what he was: the son of the wind, mightiest of the mighty, able to leap oceans and shake mountains, the one being in all the search who could do the impossible thing that now had to be done.

There is a deep meaning in this, and the tellers dwell on it, for the rousing of Hanumān is a parable of something true about all of us, in smaller measure. Hanumān had the power all along; it was in him from his birth; but he did not know it, and because he did not know it, he could not use it, and he sat helpless among the helpless while the very power that could save them all slept forgotten within him. And it took another, a wise friend who saw what Hanumān could not see in himself, to remind him of his own greatness, to call him to remember what he was, and only then could the sleeping power wake and act. How many of us carry within us more than we know, powers and capacities we have forgotten or never recognized, that wait only for the moment of need and the friend who will remind us who we are? The rousing of Hanumān tells us that our own strength may be greater than we believe, that we may be capable of far more than we have ever attempted, and that sometimes what we need is not new power but the remembering of the power we already have, and a friend wise enough to call it forth. Hanumān grew great when he remembered he was great; and the remembering was itself the beginning of the greatness.

So Hanumān stood upon the shore, grown to his full colossal stature, the son of the wind remembered and awake at last, gazing across the hundred leagues of ocean toward Lankā and toward Sītā, gathering himself for the mightiest leap the world had ever seen. The search had found its goal; the goal was across the sea; and here, at last, was the one being who could cross it. The Kishkindhā Kāṇḍa ends here, on the shore, with Hanumān poised to leap, and everything that follows, the whole triumphant flight of faith that is the Sundara Kāṇḍa, begins with this: the son of the wind, remembering his power, rising to carry the hope of Rāma across the impassable sea. · · ·

hi.title: किष्किंधा काण्ड: वानरों का गठबंधन
hi.body:
किष्किंधा काण्ड: वानरों का गठबंधन

उसने उसके आभूषण देखे

वे पंपा पहुँचे, और वह एक अत्यंत सुंदर स्थान था, फूलों से लदे वृक्षों और गाते पक्षियों से घिरा एक सरोवर, वसंत की पूर्णता में मनोहर, और उसकी यही सुंदरता राम के लिए एक यातना बन गई। क्योंकि जब हृदय शोकाकुल हो तो सुंदरता सांत्वना नहीं देती; वह घाव करती है। हर फूला हुआ वृक्ष उन्हें सीता का स्मरण कराता, जिन्हें ऐसी वस्तुएँ प्रिय थीं; हर पक्षी का गीत, हर कोमल वायु, वसंत का हर मधुर दृश्य, उनकी स्मृति जगाता और उनकी हानि को और तीखा कर देता। राम उस सुंदर सरोवर के तट पर चलते और उसकी सुंदरता से और अधिक शोकाकुल होते, और अपना दुख लक्ष्मण से कह सुनाते, और कथावाचक यहाँ हमें एक ऐसा राम देते हैं जो अब भी हानि से आहत हैं, जिनके लिए संसार की सुंदरता एक प्रकार की निष्ठुरता बन गई थी, हर सुंदर वस्तु उस सबसे सुंदर वस्तु का स्मरण दिलाती जिसे उन्होंने खो दिया था।

हमें इसे शीघ्रता से नहीं छोड़ देना चाहिए, क्योंकि यह शोक के विषय में एक सत्य और कोमल अवलोकन है, और कथा जानबूझकर यहाँ ठहरती है। जब हम सुखी होते हैं तो संसार की सुंदरता हमारे हर्ष की प्रतिध्वनि करती है; जब हम शोकाकुल होते हैं तो वही सुंदरता असह्य हो सकती है, क्योंकि वह हमारे दुख से निरपेक्ष होकर सुंदर बनी रहती है, और वह हर मोड़ पर हमें उस खोई हुई वस्तु और उस सुख का स्मरण कराती है जो अब हमारे पास नहीं। पंपा में राम वह हर शोकाकुल आत्मा हैं जिसने कभी वसंत को अपमान की तरह अनुभव किया हो, जो टूटे हृदय के साथ किसी सुंदर दिन में चला हो और उस दिन को उसकी सुंदरता के लिए ही घृणा की हो। कथा उन्हें यह पूर्णतः अनुभव करने देती है, और ऐसा करने में वह शोक के सत्य और अपने दिव्य नायक की मानवता का सम्मान करती है, जिन्होंने अपनी प्रियतमा की हानि ठीक वैसे ही सही जैसे हम अपनी हानियाँ सहते हैं।

परंतु पंपा के ऊपर ऋष्यमूक पर्वत उठा हुआ था, और उस पर्वत पर, देखते हुए, वह था जिसका नाम कबंध ने लिया था — सुग्रीव, वानरों का निर्वासित राजा, और सुग्रीव, दो शक्तिशाली सशस्त्र अजनबियों को समीप आते देखकर, भय से ग्रस्त हो गए।

क्योंकि सुग्रीव निर्वासन और आतंक में जी रहे थे। वे कभी वानरों के एक राजकुमार थे, परंतु उनके अपने भाई वाली, किष्किंधा के शक्तिशाली राजा, उनके विरुद्ध हो गए थे, उन्हें निकाल बाहर किया था, उनका राज्य और यहाँ तक कि उनकी पत्नी तक छीन ली थी, और अब उनका पीछा कर रहे थे, जिससे सुग्रीव ऋष्यमूक पर एक शिकार किए गए भगोड़े का जीवन जी रहे थे — वह एकमात्र स्थान जहाँ वाली नहीं आ सकते थे — मुट्ठी भर विश्वासपात्र साथियों से घिरे, सदा सतर्क, सदा भयभीत। और अब यहाँ दो अजनबी आ रहे थे, सशस्त्र, शक्तिशाली, स्पष्टतः योद्धा, उनके आश्रय की ओर बढ़ते हुए, और सुग्रीव का भय तुरंत सबसे बुरे निष्कर्ष पर जा पहुँचा: कि ये वाली द्वारा भेजे गए हत्यारे हैं, उनके भाई के एजेंट, अंततः उन्हें उनके पर्वतीय शरणस्थल में ही मार डालने आए हैं।

वे उन्हें आशंका से देखते रहे, और यह निश्चय नहीं कर पा रहे थे कि क्या करें, और यह उनके सबसे बुद्धिमान मंत्री ही थे जिन्होंने उन्हें संभाला और विषय को सुलझाया। क्योंकि सुग्रीव के मुट्ठी भर विश्वासपात्र साथियों में एक ऐसे भी थे जो विश्वासपात्र से कहीं बढ़कर, बुद्धिमान से कहीं बढ़कर थे, एक ऐसे जो, यद्यपि सुग्रीव अभी पूरी तरह नहीं जानते थे, इस युग के महानतम प्राणियों में से थे: हनुमान, वायु के पुत्र, असीम बल, असीम भक्ति और असीम बुद्धि वाले वानर, जो अब पहली बार कथा की अग्रिम पंक्ति में कदम रखते हैं और फिर उसे कभी नहीं छोड़ेंगे, क्योंकि आगे की कथा का बड़ा भाग उन्हीं का है।

भय में आकर कोई कार्य न करें, हनुमान ने अपने स्वामी को परामर्श दिया। भय शीघ्रता से निष्कर्ष पर पहुँच जाता है, और भय प्रायः गलत होता है। हमें यह ज्ञात नहीं कि ये अजनबी शत्रु ही हैं; वे उतनी ही सहजता से मित्र भी हो सकते हैं। बुद्धिमानी का मार्ग न तो भाग जाना है और न आक्रमण करना, अपितु किसी भी बात का निश्चय करने से पहले सत्य जान लेना है। मुझे भेजें, वेश बदलकर, कि मैं उनके पास जाऊँ और उनसे बात करूँ, और जान लूँ कि वे कौन हैं और क्या चाहते हैं, और तब हम जान पाएँगे कि उनसे भयभीत हों या उनका स्वागत करें। मुझे पहले भेजें कि सत्य जान सकूँ, और ज्ञान पर कार्य करें, भय पर नहीं।

यह बुद्धिमत्तापूर्ण परामर्श था, वही बुद्धि जो लगभग गुह की भी रही थी जब उन्होंने भरत की सेना का सामना किया था, और वही जिसने लक्ष्मण की शंकाओं को संभाला था — वह बुद्धि जो कहती है: प्रहार करने से पहले जानो, निर्णय लेने से पहले खोजो, सत्य के बोलने से पहले भय को कथा न लिखने दो। और सुग्रीव, हनुमान पर उतना विश्वास करते हुए जितना किसी और पर नहीं करते थे, सहमत हो गए, और हनुमान को पर्वत से नीचे भेजा कि वे अजनबियों से मिलें और उनका उद्देश्य जानें।

तब हनुमान ने एक भटकते हुए भिक्षु का रूप धारण किया, एक विनम्र तपस्वी का वेश, ऐसा छद्मवेश जो उन्हें अजनबियों को भयभीत किए बिना उनके निकट जाने और उन्हें बातचीत में खींचने देता, और वे राम और लक्ष्मण से मिलने नीचे गए, यह जाने बिना कि वे उस एकमात्र प्राणी से मिलने जा रहे हैं जिसे वे अपने शेष समस्त अस्तित्व समर्पित कर देंगे, जिसकी सेवा उनका गौरव और उनका आनंद और उनका सच्चा अर्थ बनेगी, वह प्रभु जिनके लिए, इस भेंट से आगे, हनुमान बार-बार असंभव कार्य करेंगे, समुद्र लाँघते हुए और पर्वत उठाते हुए और अपने एकल निष्ठावान हृदय में समस्त उद्देश्य की आशा वहन करते हुए। वायुपुत्र दो अजनबियों की टोह लेने पर्वत से नीचे गए, और लौटे तो अपने भगवान को पा चुके थे, यद्यपि न तो वे और न ही राम अभी जानते थे कि यह भेंट क्या थी, या यह अंततः क्या बन जाएगी।

और इसमें एक औचित्य है, कथावाचक कहते हैं, कि हनुमान पहले एक विनम्र भिक्षु के रूप में आए, छद्मवेश में, दूसरे की आवश्यकता की सेवा में, सतर्क और शिष्ट और बुद्धिमान। क्योंकि यही हनुमान थे, अपने असीम बल के नीचे: एक सेवक, परिपूर्ण सेवक, जिनकी सारी महानता भक्ति में थी, अपने विशाल गुणों को अपने लिए नहीं अपितु उनके लिए उड़ेल देने में जिन्हें वे प्रेम करते और जिनकी सेवा करते थे। वे विनम्रता के वेश में आए क्योंकि विनम्रता ही उनका सत्य था, और वे सेवा में आए क्योंकि सेवा ही उनका स्वभाव था, और वानरों में सबसे महान झुककर कथा में प्रविष्ट हुए, छद्मवेश में, अपनी शक्ति प्रदर्शित करने नहीं अपितु यह जानने कि वे कैसे सहायता कर सकते हैं। यह परिपूर्ण भक्त का परिपूर्ण परिचय है, और हनुमान जो कुछ भी आगे बनेंगे — समुद्र लाँघने वाले, लंका के दाहक, पर्वत उठाने वाले — वह सब उस पहले विनम्र, सतर्क, आत्म-विलोपी प्रयास में पहले से विद्यमान था, वह सेवक जो चुपचाप पर्वत से नीचे जा रहा था यह जानने कि वह कैसे सेवा कर सकता है।

वह भेंट होने को थी जो राम, सुग्रीव और हनुमान को एक साथ बाँध देगी, सारी कथा की धारा मोड़ देगी, महान खोज और महान युद्ध को गति देगी, और राम तथा हनुमान के बीच उस मित्रता का आरंभ करेगी जो शायद इस सुंदर और भयावह कथा में सबसे सुंदर वस्तु है। पर्वत से नीचे वायुपुत्र गए, अपने भिक्षु-वेश में, उस सुंदर निष्ठुर सरोवर के तट पर उन दो शोकाकुल अजनबियों की ओर, और कथा का अगला युग आरंभ हुआ।

सुग्रीव की शंकाओं का समाधान

हनुमान अपने भिक्षु-वेश में उन दोनों अजनबियों के पास आए, और उनसे बात की, और पहले ही शब्दों से उनके बीच एक प्रकार की पहचान उत्पन्न हुई, क्योंकि हनुमान बुद्धिमान थे, और राम राम थे, और दोनों ने तुरंत जान लिया कि यहाँ कोई साधारण प्राणी नहीं है। हनुमान का वचन इतना वाक्पटु, इतना सुगठित, इतना पूर्णतः शिष्ट और सुव्यवस्थित था कि राम उस पर चकित रह गए, और लक्ष्मण से कहा कि जो इस प्रकार बोल सकता है वह अवश्य ही उच्चतम संस्कार वाला प्राणी होगा, कि भाषा पर ऐसा अधिकार दुर्लभ गुण वाले मन का द्योतक है। और हनुमान ने, अपनी ओर से, अजनबियों को बोलने के लिए प्रेरित करते हुए, उनकी कथा जान ली: कि यह अयोध्या के राजकुमार राम थे, जिनकी पत्नी को एक राक्षस हर ले गया था, जो उसे पुनः पाने के लिए सहायक ढूँढ़ रहे थे, और जिन्हें मरणासन्न कबंध ने सुग्रीव के पास भेजा था।

और जब हनुमान समझ गए कि ये कौन हैं और क्या चाहते हैं, तो उनका छद्मवेश और उनकी सतर्कता उतर गई, क्योंकि उन्होंने तुरंत देख लिया कि यहाँ सुग्रीव के लिए कोई खतरा नहीं अपितु स्वयं उनका उद्धार खड़ा है, मानो नियति द्वारा भेजा गया एक सहायक, जिसकी आवश्यकता सुग्रीव की अपनी आवश्यकता से मेल खाती थी और जिसकी शक्ति सुग्रीव की हर खोई हुई वस्तु को लौटा सकती थी। उन्होंने अपना स्वरूप प्रकट किया, और उन्हें सुग्रीव के विषय में बताया, उनके निर्वासन और उनके साथ हुए अन्याय के विषय में, कि कैसे उनके भाई वाली ने उन्हें निकाल बाहर किया था और उनका राज्य तथा उनकी पत्नी छीन ली थी, और कैसे सुग्रीव भी एक ऐसे सहायक के लिए तरसते थे जो उन्हें उनकी खोई हुई वस्तुएँ पुनः दिला सके। यहाँ, हनुमान ने देखा, स्वर्ग में रची गई मित्रता थी: दो अन्यायग्रस्त और निर्वासित राजकुमार, प्रत्येक ने पत्नी और घर खोया था, प्रत्येक को ठीक वही चाहिए था जो दूसरा दे सकता था। और हनुमान, अत्यंत हर्षित होकर, दोनों भाइयों को सुग्रीव से मिलाने पर्वत पर ऊपर ले गए, और इस प्रकार गठबंधन का आरंभ हुआ।

सुग्रीव और राम मिले, और उनकी भेंट उष्ण थी, क्योंकि प्रत्येक ने दूसरे में एक सहदुखी और स्वाभाविक सहयोगी को पहचाना, और उन्होंने मित्रता की प्रतिज्ञा करने का निश्चय किया, और उन्होंने यह सबसे गंभीर रीति से किया — अग्नि के समक्ष। उन्होंने एक पवित्र अग्नि प्रज्वलित की, और उसके चारों ओर मित्रता और गठबंधन की शपथ ली, प्रत्येक ने दूसरे को उसकी खोई हुई वस्तु पुनः प्राप्त करने में सहायता का वचन दिया: राम सुग्रीव को वाली को पराजित कर उनका राज्य और पत्नी पुनः पाने में सहायता करेंगे; सुग्रीव अपने वानरों की विशाल सेना राम की सेवा में लगाएँगे, सीता को खोजने और उन्हें पुनः प्राप्त करने में सहायता के लिए। यह अग्नि द्वारा मुहरबंद प्रतिज्ञा थी, सबसे बाध्यकारी शपथ, और इसने उस क्षण से दोनों को और उनके उद्देश्यों को एक साथ बाँध दिया।

और सुग्रीव ने, अपनी आशा जगते हुए, राम को एक वस्तु दिखाई जो उन्होंने सँभाल रखी थी: क्योंकि वे उन में से थे जो पर्वत-शिखर पर उपस्थित थे जब रावण सीता को लेकर ऊपर से उड़ा था, और उन्होंने आभूषणों की वह पोटली देखी थी जो उसने गिराई थी, और उसे उठाकर सँभाल रखा था। अब उन्होंने उसे निकालकर राम को दिखाया, वे आभूषण जो सीता ने संकेत के रूप में नीचे गिराए थे। और राम ने उन्हें देखकर पहचान लिया कि वे सीता के हैं, और फिर से शोक और प्रेम से अभिभूत हो गए, अपनी खोई हुई पत्नी के आभूषण थामे, वह पहला स्पर्शनीय चिह्न जो उन्होंने उसका पाया था, यह प्रमाण कि वह इस मार्ग से गई थी, कि वह जीवित है, कि उसे ठीक वैसे ही दक्षिण की ओर ले जाया गया था जैसा जटायु ने कहा था। उन्होंने आभूषणों को अपने हृदय से लगाया और उन पर रोए, और उनका यह शोक देखकर सुग्रीव और हनुमान द्रवित हो गए और उनके उद्देश्य से और दृढ़ता से बँध गए।

परंतु एक कठिनाई थी, और सुग्रीव, प्रतिज्ञा कर लेने पर भी, एक शंका से व्याकुल थे, और उनकी शंका उचित थी, और उसका समाधान ही इस अध्याय का सार है। क्योंकि सुग्रीव ने राम की सहायता करने की प्रतिज्ञा की थी, परंतु राम ने वाली के विरुद्ध सुग्रीव की सहायता करने की प्रतिज्ञा की थी, और वाली भयंकर थे। वाली समस्त वानरों में सबसे शक्तिशाली थे, ऐसे बल के जो प्रसिद्ध था, और सुग्रीव उनसे असहाय भय में भाग गए थे और एक शिकार किए गए निर्वासित का जीवन इसीलिए जी रहे थे क्योंकि वे अपने भाई की शक्ति के समक्ष टिक नहीं सकते थे। और अब यहाँ राम थे, इसी वाली को पराजित करने का वचन देते हुए; परंतु राम एक अजनबी थे, एक मनुष्य, और सुग्रीव अभी नहीं जानते थे कि क्या राम का बल भी वाली के बल के समान है। उन्होंने इस गठबंधन पर सब कुछ दाँव पर लगा दिया था, परंतु शंका की एक फुसफुसाहट शेष रह गई थी: क्या यह सहयोगी, अपनी संपूर्ण उदात्त मुद्रा के बावजूद, वास्तव में उतना शक्तिशाली था जितना उसने वचन दिया था? या क्या सुग्रीव, उन पर विश्वास करके, स्वयं को पुनः अपने भयंकर भाई के समक्ष एक ऐसे चैंपियन के साथ खड़ा पाएँगे जो उसकी बराबरी नहीं कर सकता?

राम ने इस शंका को समझा, और इसका बुरा नहीं माना, क्योंकि यह उचित थी, और उन्होंने इसका उत्तर शब्दों से नहीं अपितु प्रमाण से देने का निश्चय किया। और इस प्रकार उन्होंने दो कार्य किए जिन्होंने सुग्रीव की हर हिचकिचाहट का लेशमात्र भी बहा दिया, और वे प्रसिद्ध हैं।

सुग्रीव ने राम को दुंदुभि नामक एक राक्षस का विशाल कंकाल दिखाया, एक भयंकर भैंसा-राक्षस जिसे वाली ने बहुत पहले मार डाला था और जिसकी विशाल शुष्क हड्डियाँ अब भी वहीं पड़ी थीं जहाँ वे गिरी थीं। यह वाली के बल की एक माप थी कि उन्होंने ऐसे विशाल प्राणी को मार डाला था; और सुग्रीव, वह विशाल कंकाल दिखाकर, राम को यह बताना चाहते थे कि वे किसका सामना करने जा रहे हैं। और राम ने, उत्तर में, बस उस विशाल कंकाल के पास चलकर गए, और अपने एक ही पैर की ठोकर से, हड्डियों के उस समूचे विशाल ढेर को वायु में उड़ा दिया, उसे अपार दूरी तक फेंक दिया, उस भयंकर कंकाल को ऐसे उछाला जैसे कोई बालक गेंद उछालता हो। यह सहज, अभिभूत करने वाले बल का प्रदर्शन था, और सुग्रीव की आँखें विस्फारित हो गईं, परंतु शंका की एक छाया शेष रही, क्योंकि उन्होंने तीक्ष्णता से देखा कि वाली ने दुंदुभि को तब मारा था जब वह राक्षस जीवित था और अपने पूर्ण बल में था, जबकि राम ने केवल शुष्क मृत हड्डियों को फेंका था; ये कार्य पूर्णतः समान नहीं थे।

अतः राम ने उन्हें दूसरा प्रमाण दिया, और इसने किसी भी शंका के लिए कोई स्थान शेष नहीं छोड़ा। निकट ही सात विशाल साल वृक्षों की एक पंक्ति खड़ी थी, एक सीध में शक्तिशाली तने। और राम ने अपना धनुष उठाया, और एक ही बाण जोड़ा, और खींचा, और छोड़ा, और वह एक बाण उन सातों विशाल वृक्षों को, एक के बाद एक, आर-पार भेद गया, प्रत्येक को छेदता हुआ, और आगे पृथ्वी में से भी निकल गया, और, कथावाचक कहते हैं, राम के तूणीर में लौट आया। एक ही शर से भेदे गए सात विशाल वृक्ष: यह वाली के किसी भी कार्य से परे उपलब्धि थी, सुग्रीव ने जो कुछ भी कभी देखा या कल्पना की थी उससे परे, ऐसी शक्ति का प्रदर्शन जो सामान्य से इतनी दूर थी कि वह केवल किसी मनुष्येतर प्राणी की ही हो सकती थी।

और इसके साथ ही, सुग्रीव की हर शंका बह गई, और उनकी हिचकिचाहट एक हर्षित, अभिभूत करने वाले विश्वास में बदल गई। वे अब समझ गए कि उनका सहयोगी कोई साधारण योद्धा नहीं था, चाहे कितना ही उदात्त हो, अपितु एक ऐसी शक्ति थी जिसके समक्ष भयंकर वाली भी कुछ नहीं थे, और यह कि राम से बँधकर उन्होंने स्वयं को निश्चित विजय से बाँध लिया था। वे राम के चरणों में गिर पड़े, विस्मय और कृतज्ञता और आशा से भरकर, अब बिना किसी भय के अपने भाई के विरुद्ध जाने को तत्पर, इस बात का निश्चय करते हुए कि ऐसे चैंपियन के साथ उनका दीर्घ निर्वासन समाप्त हो रहा है और उनका चुराया हुआ राज्य तथा पत्नी लौटा दी जाएगी। प्रतिज्ञा मुहरबंद हुई, शंका दूर हुई, गठबंधन दृढ़ हुआ, और वे दोनों अन्यायग्रस्त राजकुमार, एक-दूसरे से बलवान होकर, अब अपनी मित्रता की पहली आवश्यकता की ओर मुड़े: वाली को चुनौती देने की, और उस भयंकर, नैतिक दृष्टि से विचलित करने वाले युद्ध की ओर जो वानरों में सबसे शक्तिशाली की मृत्यु और सुग्रीव के सिंहासन पर पुनर्स्थापन में समाप्त होगा।

वाली का वध

योजना अपनी रूपरेखा में सरल थी। सुग्रीव किष्किंधा जाकर वाली को एकल द्वंद्व की चुनौती देंगे, और जब भाई युद्ध करेंगे, राम, समीप ही छिपे हुए, वह बाण छोड़ेंगे जो वाली का वध करेगा, और इस प्रकार सुग्रीव अपने भयंकर भाई से मुक्त होकर अपने राज्य पर पुनर्स्थापित हो जाएँगे। परंतु इसका क्रियान्वयन पहली बार में गलत हो गया, और यह गलत होना, और फिर सुधारा जाना, और सबसे बढ़कर वह गहन नैतिक प्रश्न जो यह संपूर्ण प्रसंग उठाता है, इसे संपूर्ण महाकाव्य के सबसे विवादास्पद अध्यायों में से एक बनाते हैं।

सुग्रीव गए और वाली को चुनौती दी, और वाली बाहर आए, और दोनों भाई युद्ध करने लगे, और वे ऐसी उग्रता और ऐसी समानता से लड़े कि राम, अपने छिपने के स्थान से देखते हुए, धनुष खींचे हुए, उन्हें एक-दूसरे से अलग नहीं पहचान सके। क्योंकि दोनों वानर भाई रूप में इतने समान थे, धूल में जूझते और घूमते हुए, कि राम ने अपना बाण छोड़ने का साहस नहीं किया, इस भय से कि कहीं वाली के बदले सुग्रीव को न लग जाए। और इसलिए उन्होंने अपना हाथ रोक लिया, और युद्ध चलता रहा, और वाली, कहीं अधिक बलवान, सुग्रीव को बुरी तरह पीटने लगे, और सुग्रीव, घायल और यह देखकर भ्रमित कि उनके सहयोगी ने प्रहार नहीं किया, युद्ध छोड़कर विषाद में राम के पास भाग आए।

तुमने बाण क्यों नहीं छोड़ा, सुग्रीव ने घायल और उलाहना भरे स्वर में पूछा। तुमने वचन दिया था, और मैंने तुम पर विश्वास किया, और मैं उस वचन के बल पर अपने भाई के विरुद्ध गया, और उसने मुझे लगभग मार ही डाला, और तुम्हारा बाण कभी नहीं आया। और राम ने समझाया: मैं तुम दोनों को अलग नहीं पहचान सका। तुम इतने समान हो कि मुझे भय था कि उसके बदले तुम्हें ही न लग जाए। पुनः जाओ, परंतु इस बार अपने को अलग पहचानने योग्य कोई वस्तु धारण करो, कोई चिह्न, कोई माला, ताकि मैं युद्ध में तुम्हें पहचान सकूँ और सही भाई पर प्रहार करूँ। और इस प्रकार व्यवस्था की गई; हनुमान ने, या किसी अन्य ने, सुग्रीव के गले में फूलों की एक माला डाल दी, ताकि दूसरे युद्ध में राम दोनों भाइयों को अलग पहचान सकें।

सुग्रीव पुनः गए, और पुनः वाली को चुनौती दी, और पुनः दोनों भाई युद्ध करने लगे, और इस बार राम, देखते हुए, माला को देख सके और अपने मित्र को पहचान सके, और जब क्षण आया उन्होंने अपना धनुष खींचा और अपने छिपने के स्थान से बाण छोड़ा, और वह शर सीधा उड़ा और वाली की छाती में जा लगा, और वानरों में सबसे शक्तिशाली गिर पड़े।

और अब वह क्षण आता है जिसने विचारशील पाठकों को इस कथा के कहे जाने के समय से ही व्याकुल किया है, क्योंकि वाली, मरणासन्न पड़े हुए, चुपचाप नहीं मरे, अपितु राम पर एक कटु और शक्तिशाली आरोप के साथ मुड़े, और उस आरोप का उत्तर देना सरल नहीं था। राम अपने छिपने के स्थान से बाहर आए, और वाली ने, मरते हुए, ऊपर उनकी ओर देखा और उनकी धार्मिकता को सामने से ललकारा। तुम राम हो, वाली ने कहा, या उनके मरणासन्न शब्दों का यही भाव था, इक्ष्वाकु के महान कुल के राजकुमार, अपने न्याय के लिए, अपने सद्गुण के लिए, अपने अटूट धर्म के लिए संपूर्ण संसार में विख्यात। लोग तुम्हारा नाम धार्मिकता की कसौटी के रूप में लेते हैं। और तुमने उस धार्मिकता का मेरे विरुद्ध कैसे उपयोग किया है? तुमने मुझे छिपकर, घात लगाकर गोली मारी, जब मैं किसी अन्य से युद्धरत था और तुमसे मेरा कोई विवाद न था और मैंने तुम्हें देखा तक नहीं था। मैंने तुम्हारा कोई अनिष्ट नहीं किया था। मैंने तुम्हें या तुम्हारे किसी को कभी हानि नहीं पहुँचाई थी। तुम्हारे पास मेरे विरुद्ध कोई कारण न था। और फिर भी तुमने, धर्म के दर्पण ने, मुझे छिपकर मार गिराया, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे कोई शिकारी जलाशय पर किसी पशु को बिना चेतावनी दिए, बिना चुनौती दिए, बिना उसे सामने आने का कोई अवसर दिए गोली मार देता है। इसमें तुम्हारी वह प्रशंसित धार्मिकता कहाँ है? कौन-सा योद्धा-नियम, कौन-सी सम्मान-संहिता किसी राजा को यह अनुमति देती है कि वह किसी ऐसे प्राणी को घात लगाकर मार दे जिसने उसका कोई अनिष्ट न किया हो? तुमने अपने महान नाम को एक कायर के कृत्य से कलंकित किया है, और मैं, मरते हुए, जानना चाहता हूँ कि तुम इसे कैसे उचित ठहराते हो।

यह एक सशक्त आरोप था, और उसका बल वास्तविक है, और कथा यह ढोंग नहीं करती कि वह नहीं है। राम ने एक ऐसे प्राणी को छिपकर मारा था जिसका उनसे कोई विवाद न था; ऊपरी दृष्टि से, यह ठीक वैसा ही अन्याय प्रतीत होता है जैसा वाली कहते हैं। और राम का उत्तर, वह औचित्य जो वे देते हैं, संपूर्ण महाकाव्य के सबसे गहन नैतिक तर्क के अंशों में से एक है, और उस पर ध्यानपूर्वक विचार करना उचित है, क्योंकि यह राम एक वास्तविक कठिन प्रकरण से अपने तर्क द्वारा गुजरते हुए हैं, जैसा वे सदैव करते हैं, केवल शक्ति या केवल दावे पर विषय को टिकने देने से इनकार करते हुए।

राम मरणासन्न वाली के पास घुटने टेककर बैठे और उन्हें उत्तर दिया। मुझे सुनो, उन्होंने कहा, क्योंकि तुम एक उत्तर के अधिकारी हो, और मैं तुम्हें एक सच्चा उत्तर दूँगा। तुम मुझ पर अन्याय का आरोप लगाते हो, परंतु विचार करो कि तुमने क्या किया है, और मेरा कर्तव्य क्या है। तुमने एक गंभीर पाप किया है, स्वयं धर्म की व्यवस्था के विरुद्ध पाप, क्योंकि तुमने अपने ही भाई को निकाल बाहर किया और, जब वह जीवित था, उसकी पत्नी को अपने लिए ले लिया। भाई के जीवित रहते उसकी पत्नी को ले लेना सबसे गंभीर अपराधों में से एक है; विधि के अनुसार यह एक भयंकर कृत्य है, नैतिक व्यवस्था की जड़ पर आघात है, और उस कृत्य से तुमने स्वयं को, राजा होते हुए भी, ऐसे पशु के स्तर पर गिरा लिया जो ऐसी किसी विधि को नहीं जानता। अब मैं इक्ष्वाकु कुल का हूँ, और यह हमारे वंश का प्राचीन कर्तव्य है कि पृथ्वी पर धर्म को बनाए रखे, जहाँ भी अपराध पाया जाए उसे दंडित करे, अपने राज्यों में भी नहीं तो अन्य राज्यों में भी, क्योंकि मेरे वंश के राजा नैतिक व्यवस्था के नियुक्त संरक्षक हैं। तुमने ऐसा पाप किया था जो दंड योग्य था, और यह मुझ पर आ पड़ा, धर्म के संरक्षक के रूप में, कि उसे दंडित करूँ। यह पहला उत्तर है: मैंने तुम पर बिना कारण नहीं अपितु एक वास्तविक और गंभीर अन्याय के न्यायोचित दंड के रूप में प्रहार किया।

और जहाँ तक इसकी रीति की बात है, छिपकर गोली मारने की, राम ने आगे कहा, इस पर भी विचार करो। तुम मनुष्य नहीं हो, योद्धाओं के बीच युद्ध की संहिताओं से बँधे हुए; तुम एक वानर हो, वन के प्राणियों में से एक, और मनुष्य वन के प्राणियों का शिकार करते हैं, और ऐसे प्राणी को किसी भी उपाय से पकड़ना, चाहे छिपकर या खुले में, जैसा शिकारी सदा से करते आए हैं, धर्म का उल्लंघन नहीं है। परंतु इससे भी अधिक: तुम्हारा बल ऐसा है कि खुले युद्ध में कोई भी तुम्हारे समक्ष टिक नहीं सकता; यही संपूर्ण कारण है कि तुम्हारे भाई तुमसे भाग गए और तुम्हारा सामना नहीं कर सके। यदि मैंने तुम्हें खुले में चुनौती दी होती, तो तुम बस मुझ पर हावी हो जाते या भाग जाते, और तुम्हारे पाप को जो दंड चाहिए था वह कभी पूरा न हो पाता। ऐसे अपराधी को दंडित करने के लिए जो खुले युद्ध में पकड़े जाने के लिए अत्यंत शक्तिशाली हो, न्यायकर्ता वह उपाय अपना सकता है जो कार्य करे, जैसे शिकारी बलवान पशु के विरुद्ध छिपाव का उपयोग करता है। लक्ष्य न्यायोचित था, और साधन वैसे थे जैसे प्रकरण ने अनुमति दी।

अब हमें उतने ही ईमानदार होना चाहिए जितनी कथा स्वयं ईमानदार है, कि हर पाठक को राम का उत्तर पूर्णतः संतोषजनक नहीं लगा है, और वाली-वध पर विवाद कभी पूर्णतः सुलझा नहीं है, और शायद यह सुलझाने के लिए बना ही नहीं है। इसमें एक असहजता है जिसे यह तर्क पूर्णतः विलीन नहीं करता, और कथा मानो चाहती है कि हम उस असहजता को अनुभव करें, उससे जूझें, न कि किसी सरल समाधान को स्वीकार कर लें। क्योंकि यहाँ इस प्रसंग के गहन उद्देश्यों में से एक है: यह हमें दिखाता है कि स्वयं राम भी, स्वयं धार्मिकता की कसौटी भी, एक ऐसे संसार में कार्य करते हैं जहाँ धर्म सदैव सरल नहीं होता, जहाँ सही मार्ग सदैव निष्कलंक नहीं होता, जहाँ नैतिक व्यवस्था को बनाए रखने के लिए ऐसे कृत्य आवश्यक हो सकते हैं जो न्याय की सेवा करते हुए भी अंतःकरण को व्याकुल करते हैं। संसार सुव्यवस्थित नहीं है। सबसे उत्तम पुरुष भी, सत्य की सेवा करने का अपना सच्चा प्रयास करते हुए, ऐसे ढंग से कार्य कर सकता है जिस पर एक शुद्ध अंतःकरण प्रश्न उठा सके। और कथा, वाली को इतना सशक्त आरोप और राम को इतना तर्कसंगत परंतु पूर्णतः असहज न करने वाला उत्तर देकर, यह ढोंग करने से इनकार करती है कि धार्मिकता कभी सरल होती है या धर्म के सेवक इस पतित संसार में कर्म की कठिन जटिलताओं से बच पाते हैं। यह कथा का दोष नहीं है; यह उसकी ईमानदारी है, राम को सहज पूर्णता के प्रतीक के बजाय एक ऐसी आत्मा बनाने से इनकार करना जो वास्तव में, जैसे हम सबको करना पड़ता है, सही करने की भयंकर कठिनाई से जूझ रही है।

और वाली स्वयं, अंततः, संतुष्ट हो गए, और यह महत्वपूर्ण है, क्योंकि जिसके पास राम की सबसे अधिक निंदा करने का कारण था वही, मरते हुए, इस बात की न्यायसंगतता को स्वीकार करने आए कि क्या किया गया था। राम का उत्तर सुनकर, अंततः अपने ही पाप की गंभीरता और अपने दंड की न्यायसंगतता को समझते हुए, उस नैतिक व्यवस्था के गहरे सत्य को जिसका उन्होंने उल्लंघन किया था, वाली की कटुता दूर हो गई। उन्होंने राम के शब्दों की सत्यता स्वीकार की, अपने ही अपराध और अपने कठोर आरोप के लिए क्षमा माँगी, और, मरते हुए, राम को उस वस्तु की देखभाल सौंप दी जिसे वे संसार में सबसे अधिक प्रेम करते थे — अपने पुत्र अंगद — यह विनती करते हुए कि बालक की रक्षा और लालन-पालन किया जाए। और इस प्रकार वाली समाधान में मरे, उनकी शत्रुता समझ में विलीन होकर, अपने पुत्र को उसी के हाथों सौंपकर जिसके बाण ने उनका वध किया था, अंततः उस न्याय से शांति पाकर जिसने उन्हें गिरा दिया था। और राम ने अंगद का भार ग्रहण किया, और उसका सम्मान किया, और वानरों में सबसे शक्तिशाली संसार से चले गए, अपना राज्य उस भाई को छोड़कर जिसके साथ उन्होंने अन्याय किया था और अपने पुत्र को उस प्रभु के संरक्षण में छोड़कर जिसने उनका न्याय किया था।

तारा का शोक

वाली मर चुके थे, और किष्किंधा, जो उनके शक्तिशाली शासन में हर्षित रहा था, शोक में डूब गया, और उस शोक के केंद्र में उनकी विधवा तारा खड़ी थीं, और उनका विलाप महाकाव्य के महान विलापों में से एक है, और उनका चरित्र इसके सबसे प्रशंसनीय चरित्रों में से एक है।

तारा वाली की महारानी थीं, और वे कोई साधारण पत्नी न थीं। वे बुद्धिमान थीं, राज्य के अधिकांश मंत्रियों से भी अधिक बुद्धिमान, और कहा जाता है कि उन्होंने वाली को उसी युद्ध के विरुद्ध चेतावनी दी थी जिसने उन्हें मार डाला, उन्होंने परामर्श दिया था कि सुग्रीव के विरुद्ध दूसरी बार बाहर न जाएँ, क्योंकि उन्होंने तीक्ष्णता से यह तर्क किया था कि सुग्रीव अपने शक्तिशाली भाई को पुनः चुनौती देने का साहस तब तक न करते जब तक उन्होंने कोई शक्तिशाली सहयोगी न पा लिया हो, और यह कि बुद्धिमानी का मार्ग सावधानी था, न कि वह उतावला अभिमान जिसने वाली को अपनी मृत्यु की ओर भेजा। उन्होंने नहीं सुना था। शक्तिशाली प्रायः सावधानी के परामर्श को नहीं सुनते, और वाली ने अपने बल में अपनी बुद्धिमान पत्नी की चेतावनी का तिरस्कार किया और बाहर जाकर मर गए, और अब तारा की बुद्धिमत्ता सबसे कटु ढंग से सिद्ध हुई, उसी मृत्यु से जिसे उन्होंने पूर्वदृष्ट किया था और रोक नहीं पाई थीं।

वे वहाँ आईं जहाँ वाली मरणासन्न पड़े थे, या मर चुके थे, और वे उनके शरीर पर गिर पड़ीं, और वे रोईं, और कथन में उनका विलाप दीर्घ और मर्मस्पर्शी है, एक बुद्धिमान स्त्री का शोक उस पति के लिए जिसे उसने प्रेम किया था और चेतावनी दी थी और खो दिया था। उन्होंने भाग्य के विरुद्ध वैसे नहीं चिल्लाया जैसे कोई मूर्ख स्त्री कर सकती थी; उनका शोक गहन था परंतु समझ से रहित नहीं था; उन्होंने त्रासदी का संपूर्ण रूप देखा — अपने पति का अभिमान, अपनी अनसुनी चेतावनी, उस नियति का घटित होना जिसे बुद्धि ने झलक पाई थी और प्रेम रोक नहीं सका था। और उन्होंने, अपने शोक में, राज्य के उस संपूर्ण व्यवसाय की उपेक्षा की जो उनके चारों ओर घूम रहा था, उत्तराधिकार और सत्ता के वे प्रश्न जो वाली की मृत्यु ने खोल दिए थे; उन्हें उस समय इस बात की कोई चिंता न थी कि कौन शासन करेगा; उन्हें केवल इसकी चिंता थी कि उनके पति मर चुके थे, और उन्होंने अपने संपूर्ण हृदय से उनका शोक मनाया, ऐसी गरिमा के साथ जिसने उनके पतन का कारण बनने वालों का भी सम्मान बाध्य किया।

तारा के शोक में एक विशेष करुणा है, और उस पर ठहरना उचित है, क्योंकि यह उस बुद्धिमान का शोक है जो अपनी प्रिय वस्तु को बचा न सकी। खतरे को स्पष्ट रूप से देख लेने में, चेतावनी बोल देने में, बुद्धि जो कुछ कर सकती थी वह सब कर लेने में, और फिर प्रियजन को उस चेतावनी के आगे से गुजरकर ठीक उसी विनाश में चले जाते देखने में एक विशेष यातना है। तारा को वह यातना थी। उन्होंने जाना था; उन्होंने कहा था; और वह पर्याप्त न था; और अब उन्हें न केवल अपने पति के लिए अपितु अपनी ही स्पष्ट दृष्टि की भयंकर निरर्थकता के लिए भी शोक करना था, उस चेतावनी के लिए जो सत्य थी और सुनी न गई। सही होना और असहाय होना, चट्टान को देखना और प्रियजन को उससे मोड़ न पाना, मानवीय दुखों में सबसे कठिन दुखों में से है, और तारा ने वह दुख सहा, और कथा उन्हें उस गरिमा के लिए सम्मान देती है जिससे उन्होंने उसे सहा।

और युवा अंगद था, वाली का पुत्र, वह बालक जिसे मरणासन्न वाली ने राम की देखभाल में सौंपा था, और उसका शोक भी भयंकर था, अचानक पिताविहीन हो गए पुत्र का शोक, और एक ऐसे राजकुमार का भय जो अचानक उस राज्य में अपने स्थान के प्रति अनिश्चित हो गया था जो उसके चाचा को जाने वाला था। वानरों का संपूर्ण राजवंश अपने शक्तिशाली राजा के पतन से भ्रम और शोक में डूब गया, और कुछ समय के लिए ऐसा प्रतीत हुआ कि शोक और अनिश्चितता राज्य को छिन्न-भिन्न कर देंगे।

परंतु व्यवस्था पुनर्स्थापित होनी थी, क्योंकि कोई राज्य सदा शोक नहीं मना सकता, और जीवितों को मृतकों के छोड़े हुए विषयों की व्यवस्था करनी ही होती है। और यहाँ राम का न्याय पुनः प्रकट हुआ, और वस्तुओं की उचित व्यवस्था के प्रति उनकी सावधानी भी। वाली मर चुके थे, और अधिकारपूर्वक राज्य अब सुग्रीव को जाता था, जिनके साथ वाली ने अन्याय किया था, और सुग्रीव अंततः किष्किंधा के राजा के रूप में राज्याभिषिक्त हुए, उस सिंहासन पर पुनर्स्थापित हुए जिससे उनके भाई ने उन्हें निकाला था, उनका दीर्घ निर्वासन समाप्त हुआ। परंतु राम ने सावधानी बरती कि यह पुनर्स्थापन न्यायसंगत और संपूर्ण हो, और यह कि शक्तिशालियों के झगड़ों के लिए निर्दोष को कष्ट न उठाना पड़े। और इस प्रकार, राम के बुद्धिमान आग्रह पर, यह व्यवस्था की गई कि युवा अंगद, वाली का पुत्र, न तो त्याग दिया जाए और न विरासत से वंचित किया जाए, अपितु उसे युवराज, सुग्रीव के सिंहासन का उत्तराधिकारी बनाया जाए। इस प्रकार जिस बालक ने अपना पिता खोया था उसने अपना भविष्य नहीं खोया; उसका उत्तराधिकार सुरक्षित किया गया; और राज्य पुनः एक हो गया, सुग्रीव राजा और अंगद उत्तराधिकारी, राजवंश की दोनों शाखाएँ युद्धरत होने के बजाय पुनः जुड़ गईं।

यह एक बुद्धिमान और दयालु व्यवस्था थी, और यह चिह्नित करना उचित है कि इसने क्या सिद्ध किया। वाली की मृत्यु कटुता की विरासत छोड़ सकती थी — एक अन्यायग्रस्त विधवा, एक विरासत-वंचित पुत्र, एक ऐसा राज्य जो मृत राजा के पक्षधरों और नए राजा के पक्षधरों के बीच बँटा हुआ हो। इसके बजाय, वाली के पुत्र का सम्मान करके, अंगद के स्थान को सुरक्षित करके, पराजित कुल के साथ उस कठोरता के बजाय जो विजय प्रायः दिखाती है, न्याय और उदारता से व्यवहार करके, राम और सुग्रीव ने विभाजन को गहरा करने के बजाय उसे भर दिया, और संपूर्ण राज्य को नई व्यवस्था में विभाजित छोड़ने के बजाय एक साथ बाँध दिया। यह सच्ची राजनीति का, और सच्ची धार्मिकता का चिह्न है, कि विजय में उदार हों, पराजित को कुचलने के बजाय उसका स्थान सुरक्षित करें, दंड देने के बजाय भरें; और यह उपचारकारी व्यवस्था, जिसमें अन्यायग्रस्त विधवा का सम्मान हुआ और पिताविहीन पुत्र उत्तराधिकारी बना, राम के इस आग्रह का फल है कि एक आवश्यक मृत्यु के परिणाम में भी, न्याय और करुणा को जीवितों की व्यवस्था पर शासन करना चाहिए।

और तारा को स्वयं, वह बुद्धिमान विधवा, सम्मानित किया गया और उनका उचित स्थान दिया गया, उनकी बुद्धिमत्ता का आदर हुआ, उनकी गरिमा सुरक्षित रही। वे कथा में पुनः प्रकट होंगी, उनका परामर्श अब भी मूल्यवान, उनकी स्पष्ट दृष्टि अब भी उस राज्य की सेवा करती हुई जिसने अपने पति को खोया था; क्योंकि ऐसी बुद्धिमत्ता वाली स्त्री को अलग रखा जाना बहुत मूल्यवान था, और नई व्यवस्था में उन्हें सम्मानित और निकट रखने की बुद्धि थी। उनका शोक उन्हें नष्ट नहीं कर सका; उन्होंने उसे वहन किया, जैसे बुद्धिमान अपने दुख वहन करते हैं, और आगे बढ़ीं, क्षीण परंतु टूटी नहीं, अपनी बुद्धि को उस उद्देश्य को अर्पित करने के लिए जिससे उनके पति की मृत्यु ने उन्हें जोड़ दिया था।
